$comment: ROOT-GUARD OWNERSHIP MANIFEST (#1624, epic #1621).
Haven has guards that live OUTSIDE the tree they police: a lint under
scripts/ that polices packages/backend, a ratchet that polices
packages/frontend. Only the policed package's CI job actually runs them.
So a pull request that ONLY weakens such a guard -- widening an exemption
regex, deleting a refusal, loosening a rule -- would go green with the
guard never running, unless the CI change classifier is told that the
guard belongs to that job.
That knowledge used to be four bespoke arms of a case statement. It is
data now, and this file is the single place it lives. The classifier
(scripts/ci/change-classifier.mjs) turns each entry into a routing rule;
nothing else decides it.
FIELDS
path     Exact repo-root-relative path. NOT a glob -- see below.
jobs     The output flags whose CI jobs own this file. These are the
jobs that would actually catch a regression in it.
runsVia  The npm script(s) those jobs run to exercise the guard. This is
what makes `jobs` a CHECKED claim rather than an assertion:
scripts/ci/root-guard-ownership.test.mjs reads .github/workflows/ci.yml
and fails if a named job does not actually run one of these.
reason   Why this ownership, in a sentence someone can disagree with.
EXACT PATHS ONLY, deliberately. The epic asks for exact paths before glob
semantics, and a guard manifest is where a too-clever glob does the most
damage: `scripts/*.mjs` would silently claim every future script in that
directory for the backend job. A new guard gets a new line. The one place
globs remain is the root-CONFIG rule in the classifier (workflow files,
package.json, tsconfig*.json), which forces the full matrix rather than
naming an owner -- a different question, and its glob behaviour is
characterized by rows in scripts/ci/routing-matrix.mjs.
ADDING A GUARD: add the entry here, and add a matrix row in
scripts/ci/routing-matrix.mjs. The tests fail until you do both -- an
entry nothing exercises is the failure mode this epic exists to remove.
NOT a completeness claim. This file says where the guards it lists belong;
it does not assert that every guard in the repo is listed. Enforcing that

guards.reason: The module-boundary rule set (#982). It is authoritative over the prose in the architecture doc, so weakening a rule here is exactly the change that must re-run the gate enforcing it.
The dependency-boundary gate itself. It scans packages/backend and packages/core but is only ever run by backend_checks.
The gate's own self-test. A lint nobody tests can start passing vacuously, so loosening the test must run it.
The shrink-only ratchet that stops the positional-mock pattern growing back in packages/backend tests (#1219).
The ratchet's self-test, for the same reason as dep-lint's: a ratchet whose test is weakened can ratchet nothing.
Generates packages/core/src/api-types.ts from the backend OpenAPI spec. Backend rather than frontend despite writing into core: the drift check that would fail runs only in backend_checks.

The shared ratchet ENGINE, backing both the backend db-mock gate and the frontend wire-type gate (#1447). Routing it to one job would leave the other gate unguarded, which is the whole reason two jobs are named here.
The wire-type ratchet (#1447). It polices packages/frontend hooks and types, and only frontend_checks runs it.
Its self-test. Widening the exemption regex or deleting the --update refusal without running the gate is the specific failure this covers.
The network-map pin test (#1478) spans backend, SDK and signer sources, and all three jobs run it. Naming fewer would let a drift ship past the job that would have caught it.
